paras: The Pecaway shooting and attempted lynching took place on the night of Saturday, August 8, 1903, at Pecaway in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, when a white man named Joe Echols shot and wounded a Black man during a brawl at a political meeting. The wounded man's friends beat Echols, and a later effort to lynch the Black man was given up, so that no one was killed.
The row began as Thomas N. Williams, an independent candidate for treasurer of Pittsylvania County, was opening a speech at Pecaway.

In what a Chatham correspondent called 'a general mix-up', Echols fired five shots at the Black man, and four of them hit him, though 'not seriously'. The man's friends then 'turned upon Echols and gave him a severe beating', though they did not inflict serious wounds. Williams's audience, according to the same dispatch, 'very soon disappeared, terrorized'.

Later, 'an effort was made to lynch the negro, but cooler heads prevailed'. The report does not name the wounded man, say who made the lynching attempt or how many took part, or give a reason for the shooting.
No report of an arrest, charge or trial of Echols or of anyone involved in the lynching effort was found.

The only known account is a special dispatch from Chatham, dated August 10, printed in the Richmond Times-Dispatch on August 11 under the headline 'AN EFFORT TO LYNCH' and the subhead 'An Affray in Which a White Man Who Shot a Negro Was Beaten'. The subhead put the beating of the white shooter ahead of the shooting itself, and the item named Echols and the candidate while leaving the wounded man unnamed. No coverage of the incident appears in the Black press, and no follow-up report was found in the white press.

reader.title: Pecaway shooting and attempted lynching
bases: The only report describes a white man shooting and wounding a Black man in a brawl, after which 'an effort was made to lynch the negro' that was given up, an attempted lynching that killed no one (A1).

No one was killed: the Black man was wounded 'but not seriously' by Echols, and the later effort to lynch him was abandoned when 'cooler heads prevailed' (A1). The report does not say who made the attempt, how many took part, or why.
One Chatham special to the Richmond Times-Dispatch (A1) is the only report found; no other white or Black paper carried it.

accounts.label: Chatham correspondent
accounts.gist: A 'general mix-up' at a political meeting in which Echols shot a Black man, the man's friends beat Echols, and a later effort to lynch the Black man failed when 'cooler heads prevailed'.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined the lynching attempt ('AN EFFORT TO LYNCH') but called the shooting part of a 'general mix-up' and gave no cause or names beyond Echols's.

quotes: In a general mix-up at Pecaway, Pittsylvania county, Saturday night, Joe Echols shot five times at a negro, four shots wounding him, but not seriously.
Later an effort was made to lynch the negro, but cooler heads prevailed.
The negro's friends then turned upon Echols and gave him a severe beating, but did not inflict any serious wounds.
